title: LLM Reliability Layers Under Test: Accuracy, Yield, and the Limits of Verification
gist: A controlled test of six LLM 'reliability layers' (deterministic vocabulary check, self-correction, voting, LLM judge, refusal, human review) on the CADEC adverse-drug-event corpus finds the layers do not stack to raise accuracy: they sort answers by trustworthiness and withhold doubtful ones but correct almost none. The binding constraint is the extractor's detection (reading), and the cheapest wins came from matching annotation conventions and never asking the model to recall identifiers.

insights.claim: Stacking reliability layers around an LLM (vocabulary check, self-correction, voting, LLM-as-judge, refusal) sorted answers by trustworthiness but corrected almost none, refuting the assumption that layers are additive.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Vendors selling 'guardrail stacks' as accuracy boosters are overselling; budget for triage/routing value, not correctness gains.
insights.quote: The layers sorted the answers by how far to trust them and corrected almost none.
insights.locator: The theory: More layers should mean more accuracy

insights.claim: Majority voting over three samples of the same extractor consumed 411,000-432,000 tokens per run and changed about 27 codes a run, as many right-to-wrong as wrong-to-right, for a net effect of -1 to +1 correct answers.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Self-consistency voting can be pure token burn in extraction tasks; measure before paying for it.
insights.quote: The voter is the answerer, so a vote carries no information that the answer lacked.
insights.locator: Voting, 411,000–432,000 tokens

insights.claim: Self-correction that feeds provable failures back to the model fired only two or three times per run and corrected nothing, because the deterministic check almost never rejects what the model actually writes.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Self-refine loops may sit idle in production; check their firing rate before claiming reliability benefits.
insights.locator: Self-correction, about 1,500 tokens

insights.claim: A smaller 3.2B-parameter judge model barely distinguished right from wrong when shown only a span and code, but separated right from wrong 3.4-4.2x when shown the extractor's candidate menu, more sharply than the free vocabulary check.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: LLM-judge value depends on giving the judge the same context the generator had; context-starved judges are near-useless.
insights.locator: Second-model judge, 84,000–88,000 tokens

insights.claim: Removing the three paid layers (self-correction, voting, judge) and replaying the refusal rule changed what passed by one record on one run and by none on the other two, showing the paid layers added almost nothing beyond the free check.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Most of the reliability value in LLM pipelines can come from zero-token deterministic checks; paid layers are candidates for cost cutting.
insights.locator: Then we removed the three paid layers

insights.claim: Verdicts from different reliability layers nest rather than add: nearly everything the free check endorses the judge also endorses, so a second verdict can only remove records, never recover one the first held back.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Treat multiple verifiers as one dial trading errors vs. lost answers vs. human reviews, not a staircase of accuracy.
insights.locator: Layers withhold; they don't add

themes.theme: Yield vs accuracy and the metric trap

insights.claim: Any withholding layer raises accuracy of what passes simply by holding back answers, so accuracy flatters such layers; yield (right answers over all records) cannot be flattered and should be reported alongside accuracy.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: When evaluating AI vendors' accuracy claims, ask for yield/coverage; high accuracy on a filtered subset can hide low usefulness.
insights.quote: Accuracy alone flatters any withholding layer.
insights.locator: First, any verdict raises the accuracy

insights.claim: Passing only answers the vocabulary check marks ACCEPT let 21-23% of records through at 0.74-0.82 accuracy, while moving to that rule removed 128 errors at the cost of 49 right answers and 177 records sent for human review.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: High-precision automation of clinical/document extraction still leaves ~3/4 of records for humans; human-review cost dominates economics.
insights.locator: Refusal, 0 tokens

insights.claim: The extractor reported confidence of 1.0 on two-thirds of its answers, right or wrong, so a model-confidence threshold was useless and was retired.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: LLM self-reported confidence is not a usable gating signal; anchor trust in external deterministic artifacts.
insights.locator: Refusal, 0 tokens

insights.claim: Only the menu-shown judge's verdict produced an F1 better than shipping everything (0.420 vs 0.397) as a shipping rule.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: An informed judge is the one paid layer that may earn its tokens, but only when its verdict is actually consumed.
insights.locator: Second, the price differs by verdict

insights.claim: A bug where voting overwrote codes without re-running the vocabulary check (shipping records marked verified for codes they no longer held) left held-out F1 unchanged at 0.204 when fixed, showing precision/recall cannot distinguish an unwarranted answer from a wrong one.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Standard ML metrics can be blind to the very defects reliability engineering targets; audit metrics for what they can see.
insights.quote: We built six layers to decide which answers to trust, then scored them with a metric that cannot see the difference.
insights.locator: Defects between the layers, and inside the metric

insights.claim: The defects that mattered sat between layers and in the metric, not inside any layer: a forty-line search found three verdicts that no downstream component ever read.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Integration seams in agentic pipelines are a key failure surface; 'find the reader of every field' is a cheap audit.
insights.quote: Every layer passed its own tests.
insights.locator: Defects between the layers, and inside the metric

insights.claim: Asked to recall SNOMED codes from memory, the model invented codes that exist in no SNOMED release 13-18% of the time, answered null on up to 38% of records, and scored eight to twelve times worse than naming the concept and looking it up.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Never let an LLM emit identifiers (codes, SKUs, tickers); retrieval-plus-pick architectures are the safe design pattern.
insights.quote: Recalling the code is not weak but broken
insights.locator: We chose this shape by measuring

insights.claim: The pipeline design has the model quote each reaction while a non-LLM retriever over 227,554 SNOMED CT description rows (embedded with granite-embedding:30m) shows the model a menu of the 20 nearest concepts to pick from.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Small local embedding models plus constrained choice are enough for grounding; the value is in architecture, not bigger models.
insights.quote: The model is never asked for a code
insights.locator: The system under test: the model reads

insights.claim: Once a mention is found, the pipeline is reliable: the right concept reaches the menu for 93% of found spans and the model picks it 81% of the time.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Domain knowledge is not the bottleneck for LLM coding tasks; investment should target detection/reading.
insights.locator: Where the model loses

insights.claim: No reliability layer can add a mention the extractor missed, so the extractor's detection sets a hard ceiling: on the held-out split, just over half the annotated mentions were found (detection F1 0.521).
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Post-hoc verification cannot rescue recall; spend on better reading or a second-reader model, not more verifiers.
insights.quote: No layer can add a mention.
insights.locator: No layer can add a mention.

insights.claim: Nearly half of annotated mentions are never quoted as annotators marked them, for non-medical reasons: single words skipped, boundaries stretched, and idioms read literally.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Annotation-convention mismatch, not domain knowledge, drives benchmark scores; beware vendor claims built on domain fine-tuning.
insights.locator: Where the model loses

insights.claim: Domain-adapted models did not help: BioMistral-7B could not reliably return parseable replies and SapBERT as the retriever encoder improved the menu but worsened the final answer, whereas a worked example and a denied-reactions rule did help.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Prompt/data work beats specialized biomedical models for this workload; caution on 'vertical LLM' premiums.
insights.locator: Where the model loses

insights.claim: A supervised system (CONORM, fine-tuned on 875 of CADEC's 1,250 files) reaches end-to-end F1 of 0.72 lenient, versus 0.47-0.50 lenient for the zero-shot extractor, but still cannot say which of its answers to trust.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Fine-tuned systems still win on raw accuracy where labelled data exists; zero-shot LLMs trade accuracy for no labelling cost.
insights.locator: A supervised system does far better.

insights.claim: At temperature zero, three identical runs of gpt-oss:20b differed by four F1 points; only 70% of 233 mentions had span and code agreed across all three runs.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Even 'deterministic' LLM settings can drift; production evals need multi-run ranges, not single numbers.
insights.locator: The noise floor: three runs of the same system

insights.claim: Four other model families (llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b-instruct, qwen3:8b, granite4:micro-h) returned byte-identical output on every repeat run; gpt-oss:20b, the only mixture-of-experts model tested, was the only one that varied.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: MoE architectures may introduce batch-dependent nondeterminism; relevant for regulated workloads needing reproducibility.
insights.locator: The variation is a property of this model

insights.claim: The authors kept the nondeterministic gpt-oss:20b because it delivered 6.5 extra F1 points over llama3.1:8b.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Open-weight model choice is a reproducibility-vs-accuracy trade.
insights.locator: We kept it for its 6.5 extra points

insights.claim: Across seven further corpora and five model families, the free vocabulary check's ACCEPT lane was right 76-100% on clinical vocabularies but only 7-26% on gazetteers (place names match but are the wrong place) and never fired on financial tag names.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Lexical verification transfers to clinical coding but can reverse in geo or financial (XBRL) tagging; validate per domain.
insights.locator: Does it hold beyond CADEC?

insights.claim: On the FiNER financial corpus the model read well but coded badly, with its worst error being a habit of picking the menu's first line rather than a domain-knowledge gap.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: XBRL/financial-tagging automation needs position-bias controls in candidate menus.
insights.locator: Study the data before adding layers.

insights.claim: Seventeen experiment matrix cells ran with the wrong prompt or wrong model and were caught only because each run also saved the configuration it received.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Config-logging per run is a cheap control against silent eval errors in AI programs.
insights.locator: A fact recorded once will be wrong silently.

insights.claim: Disagreement signals (split votes, a judge saying the right answer is not on the menu, repeat-run code changes) are best used offline as a to-do list marking underspecified parts of the task, not paid for online.
insights.speaker: Pushpdeep Mishra
insights.so_what: Reposition expensive verification from inference-time to offline eval to cut LLM spend.
insights.quote: Read them offline; do not pay for them online.
insights.locator: Six practices that transfer
